mercy_translation.text:
Yet just as this had to be so, the opposite consideration again confronts us concerning what is reasonable before God: God must be shown truthful in the law concerning death. For it would be unreasonable that, for the sake of our benefit and preservation, God the Father of truth should appear false.

What, then, was to happen in this matter? What was God to do? Was he to demand repentance from human beings for their transgression? Someone might say that this would be worthy of God: just as through transgression they had come into corruption, so through repentance they might return again to incorruption.

But repentance would neither preserve what was reasonable concerning God—for he would still not be truthful if human beings were not held by death—nor does repentance recall us from what belongs to nature; it merely brings sins to an end.

If there had been only an offense and no resulting corruption, repentance would have been sufficient. But once the transgression had taken place, human beings were held in the corruption belonging to their nature and had been deprived of the grace of being according to the image. What else was required? Who was needed for such a grace and restoration except the Word of God, who in the beginning had made all things from nothing?

For it belonged to him to bring the corruptible back again to incorruption and to preserve what was fitting before the Father on behalf of all. For being the Word of the Father and above all, he alone was accordingly able to recreate all things, to suffer on behalf of all, and to intercede with the Father for all.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius does not dismiss repentance; he argues that repentance alone cannot reverse ontological corruption and death.
The chapter moves toward the necessity of the Word's restorative action.
